Anthropologists' and archeologists' work falls into four categories: research design and information collection (formulating research questions, planning and directing research, collecting information through observation, interviews, and document review, identifying sites through site reports, existing artifacts, and topographic maps, and studying archival collections); field surveys and excavation (conducting archeological surveys and exploration, laying out excavation units and clearing deposits and features under procedures, recovering artifacts and specimens, recording artifacts' exact locations and condition through drawings, photography, and three-dimensional scanning, and collecting stone, bone, metal, and other artifacts and marking their excavation locations); processing, analysis, and conservation (cleaning, restoring, and preserving artifacts, describing their materials, dimensions, shape, function, and decoration, collecting and analyzing artifacts and skeletal remains, comparing archeological data across sites, dating and identifying remains, assessing sites, and recommending protection); publication and collaboration (writing and presenting research findings, writing grant applications, teaching undergraduate and graduate students, advising governments and organizations on cultural impacts, organizing public exhibitions, and collaborating with medical, public-health, and education personnel, police, and pathologists).

Processing, analysis, dating, and identification | Turn materials into evidence | Clean, restore, and preserve artifacts, describe their materials, dimensions, shape, function, and decoration, collect and analyze artifacts and skeletal remains, compare archeological data across sites, identify and date remains, and interpret their significance.

Site assessment and protection recommendations | Connect protection with management | Assess archeological sites for resource management, development, or protection, and recommend site protection methods. Publication and teaching | Make research reviewable | Write and present research findings for professional and public audiences, write grant applications to obtain research funding, teach or supervise undergraduate and graduate students, and organize public exhibitions to promote understanding of cultural traditions.

Interdisciplinary collaboration and compliance | Work within institutional frameworks | Advise government agencies and private organizations on cultural impacts of projects and policies, collaborate with medical, public-health, and education personnel, and work with police departments and pathologists on forensic activities such as dental and skeletal structure identification. A: Green Cliff Terrace is a fictional site, locally 100×60 meters. An image report alone states that 3 pottery sherds appear on the south side and color differences on the north; no formal survey or dating, attribute, or preservation assessment exists, and no real location is provided.

B: T0501 local grid east/north/depth units are meters; zero is an arbitrary fictional datum. Recorder A on 2026-10-01; L1 lies above L2 but has disturbance. subject.name: Anthropologists and Archeologists
subject.summary: Anthropologists and archeologists correspond to US 19-3091.00. They study human origins, behavior, culture, and material remains, producing research reports, papers, and public explanations through observation, interviews, documentary or physical-material analysis. ONET lists 30 tasks (20 core/10 supplemental), including teaching, exhibitions, archival research, artifact cleaning and restoration, and forensic collaboration; a position need not perform all of them. Archeological professionals (2-10-08-01) in China's 2022 occupational classification catalogue conduct surveys, exploration, excavation, processing, assessment, and research, covering only part of the combined US occupation. BLS EP19-3091: 10,200 people in 2025 and 10,800 in 2035, growth of 6.0% over 2025–2035, an official net increase of 600 people, 800 annual average job openings, and 8.9% self-employed. Openings include replacement needs and do not equal net new jobs or an individual's chance of being hired; US projections are not extrapolated to China.
